name: vieux-malais, the language of the 7th-century Śrīvijaya inscriptions

catalog_quote: la voyelle a du malais moderne correspond ā long dans les inscriptions. Dans celles-ci, d'ailleurs, la quantité de la voyelle varie suivant qu'elle porte ou non l'accent. Ce fait, qui avait déjà été signalé par Kern (Versp. Gesch., pp. 212-213), est défini en ces termes par M. Blagden (J. Straits br. RAS., 64, p. 70) : l'addition au mot racine d'un suffixe, ou même simplement d'un enclitique, produit un déplacement de l'accent d'intensité; c'est une vieille loi indonésienne qui s'est un peu oblitérée dans le malais parlé aujourd'hui dans la Péninsule, mais l'orthographe classique du malais témoigne de son application à date ancienne; c'est ainsi que l'on a marjahāti dérivé de jāhat, datūa dérivé de dātu, etc.

Gesch., pp. 212-213), est défini en ces termes par M. Blagden (J. Straits br. RAS., 64, p. 70) : l'addition au mot racine d'un suffixe, ou même simplement d'un enclitique, produit un déplacement de l'accent d'intensité ; c'est une vieille loi indonésienne qui s'est un peu oblitérée dans le malais parlé aujourd'hui dans la Péninsule, mais l'orthographe classique du malais témoigne de son application à date ancienne ; c'est ainsi que l'on a marjahāti dérivé de jāhat, datūa dérivé de dātu, etc.
new_statements.translation: In these [the inscriptions], moreover, the quantity of the vowel varies according to whether or not it bears the accent. This fact, already noted by Kern (Versp. Gesch., pp. 212-213), is defined in these terms by Mr Blagden (J. Straits br. RAS., 64, p. 70): the addition of a suffix, or even simply of an enclitic, to the root word produces a shift of the stress accent; this is an old Indonesian law that has become somewhat obliterated in the Malay spoken today in the Peninsula, but the classical orthography of Malay bears witness to its application at an early date; thus one has marjahāti derived from jāhat, datūa derived from dātu, etc.
new_statements.citation: Coedès, George. 1930. Les inscriptions malaises de Çrīvijaya. BEFEO 30: 29-80.
new_statements.locator: p. 62 (remarks on the language of the inscriptions, pp. 60-64), first paragraph; supporting notes p. 38 (lengthening of a word-final vowel before the suffix -na 'de règle dans ces textes, cf. infra, p. 62') and lexicon entries datua (p. 70) and marjjahâti (p. 75)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened, block '==== [p. 62] ====' (file lines 298-304): the passage is there. The saved scanned differs only trivially from the reader's quote (scanned 'quantiié', '<jléjà', 'RAS. y 64', and the scanned drops the vowel-length marks: 'marjahâti dérivé de jàhat, datua dérivé de datu'); the page image persee_pages/ shows 'marjahāti dérivé de jāhat, datūa dérivé de dātu' with the long marks exactly as the reader gives them, and a live refetch of the Persée page-text endpoint for p. 62 (saved as persee_pages/, HTTP 200) contains 'accent d'intensité; c'est une vieille loi indonésienne..'. Reading: Coedès says only that vowel quantity tracks the accent and that a suffix or enclitic shifts the 'acc…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for oldm1243, so this is the first stress statement for the language rather than a refinement of an existing one: penultimate intensity accent, shifting with suffixation/encliticisation, reconstructed from the vowel-length orthography of the 7th-century Śrīvijaya inscriptions (Coedès citing Kern and Blagden 1913). It is compatible with the penultimate placement recorded for modern Malay isolects (Adelaar 1992: 9, already noted).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Coedès reads the long-vowel marks of the Indic-script inscriptions as the trace of a word-level intensity accent: the accented vowel is the one written long, and when a suffix or enclitic is added the accent (and the written length) moves rightward onto the new penultimate syllable (dātu > datūa, jāhat > marjahāti; and, p. 38, a word-final vowel is regularly lengthened before the enclitic -na). He never uses the word 'penultimate'; the penult placement is what every example and the -na rule show, so the reading is inferred from his data, with the accent itself an epigraphic inference from vowel length rather than an observed pronunciation. Domain = the whole suffixed/encliticised word.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Old Malay itself; Coedès notes only that the accent-shift law 'has become somewhat obliterated' in modern Peninsular spoken Malay while classical Malay spelling still reflects it. The whole statement rests on written vowel quantity (Indic script has no sign for the pepet, so short a may stand for e-pepet, p. 61).
new_statements.identity_note: Coedès describes the language of the four 7th-century Śrīvijaya inscriptions of Sumatra and Bangka (Kedukan Bukit 683, Talang Tuwo 684, Karang Brahi, Kota Kapur 686), which he calls 'vieux-malais' following van Ronkel (p. 61); this is the core of the Old Malay corpus, not a later (Javanese or Kedah) Old Malay text.

sources.note: Stress statements only for the modern isolects (SM p. 9: penultimate unless penult has schwa + single consonant, then final; non-phonemic; same pattern for Minangkabau, Banjar, Serawai, Iban). Old Malay is used as auxiliary evidence (p. 5; sec. 6.4 pp. 163ff. is morphological); nothing on OM or Proto-Malayic stress. p. 59 only reports Zorc's (1983) pre-PM 'accent pattern favouring the last syllable' as an explanation of SM c; p. 163 infers PM *mAr- 'was never stressed' because prefixed to disyllabic lexemes.
